The reproductive biology of the brook stickleback (Culaea inconstans) is closely tied to seasonal temperature regimes. In individuals maintained at a thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum spawning rate is observed when females produce approximately one clutch every two days, amounting to an annual output of around 182 eggs per female per year. The maximum lifespan at this temperature is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], a duration that reflects the compressed growing season of northern aquatic habitats at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. Newly independent larvae emerge with a wet weight of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter documented in other gasterosteid species. This high-frequency reproductive strategy, driven by the production of small clutches, is characteristic of many small-bodied, short-lived gasterosteids. Field studies indicate that reproductive females deposit their clutches in nests constructed and guarded by males, with each spawning event typically yielding a modest number of eggs. The estimate of 182 eggs per year [Ri = 182 eggs per year] represents the upper limit of fecundity under optimal thermal conditions and abundant food resources. Comparatively, this rate is elevated relative to congeneric species such as Gasterosteus aculeatus, reflecting the brook stickleback's adaptation to productive but ephemeral northern habitats where a compressed growing season favors rapid, continuous reproduction. Such intense reproductive output places significant energetic demands on females, which must allocate substantial resources to oocyte production over several consecutive months.

The ultimate standard length of adult brook sticklebacks reaches 8.7 centimeters [Li = 8.7 centimeters] under optimal conditions. In comparison, the standard length at puberty is 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters], marking the transition to reproductive maturity. The ultimate wet weight of adults attains 7.84 grams [Wwi = 7.84 grams], and the wet weight at puberty is 1.04 grams [Wwp = 1.04 grams]. At 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at birth is 11.5 days [ab = 11.5 days], a developmental duration that influences early growth trajectories. These morphological and life-history parameters collectively define the species' position within the Gasterosteidae, where small body size, early maturation, and high fecundity are common adaptations to variable freshwater environments.
